steps.reason: Regression command failed: mvn -B -o -pl vertx-web -am -Dtest=UtilsTest,StaticHandlerTest,StaticDirectoryListHandlerTest test

parsed_output.evidence: Root cause and sink: StaticHandlerImpl.handle() in vertx-web/src/main/java/io/vertx/ext/web/handler/impl/StaticHandlerImpl.java line 138 computes the request-derived path by decoding the URL then removing dot segments. That path is then used at StaticHandlerImpl.getFile() (lines 611-614, concatenating webRoot with the offset path) and fed to the FileSystem via isFileExisting and getFileProps through wrapInTCCLSwitch around line 266. The trust boundary crossed is attacker-controlled HTTP request path flowing into a filesystem path used to read or serve a file, with the invariant that the resolved file must stay within webRoot enforced only by the dot-removal normalization. That normalization function, Utils.removeDots in vertx-web/src/main/java/io/vertx/ext/web/impl/Utils.java (lines roughly 159-231), and its internal helpers only ever check for the forward-slash character as a path-segment delimiter; they never recognize backslash, even though Windows filesystem and NIO APIs treat backslash identically to forward slash. I empirically confirmed, by running the real Utils class directly, that decoding and then removing dots from a backslash-encoded traversal payload leaves it completely unmodified, while the equivalent forward-slash payload is correctly collapsed back toward the root. Every distinct sink or path in the alert that a complete fix must cover: (1) StaticHandlerImpl.handle() through sendStatic() and getFile() to the isFileExisting/getFileProps FileSystem sink around line 266 and lines 611-614 - the primary file-read sink exercised by this PoV, reached both when the decode-then-removeDots sequence runs directly inside handle() (the alert's first and second traces) and when the path first passes through RoutingContextImpl's normalizedPath, which itself calls the same removeDots function, before handle() re-processes it (the alert's third and fourth traces). (2) StaticHandlerImpl.sendDirectoryListing()'s construction of the parent-directory link (around lines 682-687, built via substring and replace calls), which is built from the same normalizedPath/removeDots output (the alert's second vulnerability group) - a secondary sink sharing the identical root-cause normalization defect, not independently exercised by this PoV but sharing the same fix location.
parsed_output.expected_vulnerable_behavior: The command builds vertx-web offline, compiles the PoV against the real built classes, and runs it. The PoV starts a real Vert.x HTTP server with a Router and StaticHandler serving a temp webRoot, sends real HTTP GET requests for the percent-encoded backslash traversal path and the raw backslash traversal path, and checks whether the response is HTTP 200 with the body containing the marker string that was placed in a file just outside the handler's intended request namespace. That file is reachable because the un-neutralized backslash sequence in the resolved path exactly matches the file's literal, legal-on-Linux filename. On the current vulnerable code this happens for both payload variants and the process exits 0. A control request using the equivalent forward-slash payload is expected to 404 both before and after the fix, proving the defect is specific to backslash handling and not a general absence of protection.
parsed_output.notes: Targeted alert trace: vulnerability one's first and second traces, which run directly through StaticHandlerImpl.handle()'s decode-then-removeDots call at line 138 down to the FileSystem sink around line 266, since this is the trace with the most direct, most severe, and most exploitable impact (arbitrary file disclosure via the static file server) and is the one whose fix location I could confirm against the real upstream patch. The third and fourth traces of vulnerability one, which additionally route through RoutingContextImpl's normalizePath, reach the identical Utils.removeDots defect and are covered by the same root-cause fix, since normalizePath also calls Utils.removeDots without any backslash handling; I verified this by running the exact two-pass sequence (normalizePath followed by handle's decode-then-removeDots) against the real Utils class and confirmed the backslash payload survives both passes unchanged. Vulnerability two, the sendDirectoryListing parent-link sink, was deliberately not chosen as the primary PoV target because it is a much lower-severity sink affecting only the HTML up-one-directory link text built from the same normalized path, not a filesystem read, but it shares the identical root cause and is documented in the evidence and regression_hint fields so the patcher does not fix only the primary sink. I verified the PoV's correctness by temporarily patching StaticHandlerImpl.java in this worktree with the actual fix from vert.x 3.9.4 and re-running the PoV command: it correctly flipped from exit 0, with 200 responses leaking the secret, to exit 1, with 404 responses blocking both backslash payloads, then I reverted the file back to its original vulnerable state and confirmed via git status and git diff that there was no residual change to product code. The secret file is placed as a literal, single-path-component filename containing raw backslash characters, which is legal on Linux, so the exploit's observable effect of an HTTP 200 leaking a file outside the request's intended namespace is reproducible on the Linux build container even though the underlying Windows OS-level directory escape cannot itself be demonstrated there.
parsed_output.regression_hint: Invariant a correct fix must enforce: any path derived from an incoming HTTP request must have all platform path separators, both forward slash and backslash, in raw and percent-encoded form and in both letter cases, normalized to a single canonical separator before dot-segment removal runs, and the resulting canonicalized path must never be able to reference anything outside the configured webRoot on any target operating system, Windows in particular, where backslash is a real separator. The actual upstream fix, verified against vert.x 3.9.4, inserts a replacement of backslash with forward slash inside StaticHandlerImpl.handle() between the URL-decode call and the removeDots call - that is, the fix lives at the call site, not inside Utils.removeDots itself - so a correct patch must either fix it there or, more robustly, make Utils.removeDots and normalizePath themselves treat backslash as a delimiter so every caller, including RoutingContextImpl's normalizedPath and any future callers, is protected, not just StaticHandlerImpl. Known bypass variants the fix must also block, all of which should be tested: a raw literal backslash in the request line; a percent-encoded backslash in either letter case; a double-encoded backslash; mixed separators combining forward slash and backslash in the same payload, to ensure the normalization is not order-dependent or single-pass only; the same payload reaching StaticHandlerImpl via the router's first normalization pass versus the handler's own second pass, since the alert traces show both routes into removeDots; and the sendDirectoryListing parent-link sink, which consumes the same normalizedPath/removeDots output and must be re-checked after the fix to confirm it can no longer embed un-neutralized backslash segments either.
parsed_output.summary: Created a real, end-to-end PoV proving CWE-022 path traversal in vertx-web's StaticHandler. StaticHandlerImpl.handle() computes the filesystem lookup path via Utils.removeDots(Utils.urlDecode(...)), but Utils.removeDots() only treats the forward slash as a path-segment delimiter, never the backslash. A backslash-based traversal payload (raw or percent-encoded as %5c) therefore survives normalization completely unmodified, while the equivalent forward-slash payload is correctly collapsed. On Windows, the OS honors backslash as a separator, so the untouched dot-dot segments escape webRoot when handed to the FileSystem. The PoV runs a real Vert.x Router plus StaticHandler HTTP server (the actual production classes, not a simulation) and, to make the Windows-only exploitability observable on Linux CI, places a file inside webRoot whose literal on-disk name is the raw payload string (dot dot backslash repeated then secret.txt), which is a legal single-component filename on Linux. Because the vulnerable code passes the payload through untouched, real HTTP GET requests to the encoded and raw backslash traversal paths return HTTP 200 with the secret content, while the equivalent forward-slash payload correctly returns 404. I verified the flip by temporarily applying the real upstream fix (replacing backslash with forward slash before removeDots inside StaticHandlerImpl.handle(), matching the actual vertx-web 3.9.4 fix commit): both backslash payloads then 404 and the PoV exits non-zero. On the current unpatched tree it exits 0.

parsed_output.patch_notes: Root-cause fix in vertx-web/src/main/java/io/vertx/ext/web/impl/Utils.java: at the top of removeDots(CharSequence path), if the input contains a backslash it is canonicalized to '/' (path = path.toString().replace('\\', '/')) before the existing RFC 3986 dot-segment removal logic runs. This single change protects every caller: StaticHandlerImpl.handle()'s decode-then-removeDots call (line ~138, the sink feeding getFile()/isFileExisting/getFileProps around line 266 and getFile() at lines 611-614), RoutingContextImpl.normalizedPath() -> Utils.normalizePath() -> removeDots() (used both as StaticHandlerImpl's context.normalisedPath() input and directly by sendDirectoryListing()'s parent-directory link construction at lines 682-687), so all sinks named in the alert are covered, not just the one exercised by the POV. Added two regression tests to vertx-web/src/test/java/io/vertx/ext/web/UtilsTest.java: testRemoveDotsBackslashTraversal (direct Utils.removeDots calls with raw and mixed forward/backslash traversal sequences, asserting they collapse the same way their forward-slash equivalents do) and testNormalizePathBackslashTraversal (same invariant through the normalizePath entry point used by RoutingContextImpl). Ran the full UtilsTest suite (28/28 pass, including new tests), StaticDirectoryListHandlerTest (4/4 pass), and StaticHandlerTest (56/56 pass; the only 2 errors observed, testHttp2Push/testNoHttp2Push, are pre-existing 'ALPN not available for JDK SSL/TLS engine' environment failures unrelated to this change). Also re-ran the supplied POV (.security-pipeline/pov/run_pov.sh) after the patch: both backslash payloads (raw and %5c-encoded) now return 404 instead of 200, matching the forward-slash control, while the sanity /hello.txt request still returns 200 — confirming the fix blocks the vulnerability without breaking legitimate static file serving.
parsed_output.risk_notes: Change is narrowly scoped to normalization behavior inside Utils.removeDots and adds no new public API surface. Because normalizePath()/removeDots() now also collapses backslash sequences, any legitimate request path that intentionally contains a literal backslash as a meaningful (non-separator) character would now have that backslash treated as a path separator; this matches the upstream vert.x 3.9.4 security fix's intent and is very unlikely to break real-world usage, since backslash is not a conventional character in URL paths. During verification, running the Maven build in this container caused several unrelated generated asciidoc doc files (vertx-web-client .../index.adoc for groovy/js/kotlin/ruby) to be regenerated as a side effect of the codegen annotation processor; these were reverted with `git restore` and are not part of this patch.
parsed_output.summary: Fixed CWE-022 path traversal in vertx-web's StaticHandler by making Utils.removeDots() treat backslash exactly like forward slash before performing dot-segment removal. Previously, removeDots() (and its callers Utils.normalizePath() and StaticHandlerImpl.handle()) only recognized '/' as a path separator, so a raw or percent-decoded backslash-based traversal sequence (e.g. `..\..\..\secret.txt` or `..%5c..%5c..%5csecret.txt`) sailed through the '../' checks completely unmodified, while Windows/NIO filesystem APIs honor backslash as a real separator, letting the resolved file escape webRoot. The fix is applied once at the shared root-cause function (Utils.removeDots), so it automatically covers every call path in the alert: the primary StaticHandlerImpl.handle() -> getFile() -> FileSystem sink, the RoutingContextImpl.normalizedPath() double-pass route into the same sink, and the sendDirectoryListing() parent-link sink (StaticHandlerImpl lines ~682-687), which all ultimately route through removeDots()/normalizePath(). Verified against the provided POV: before the fix both the raw-backslash and percent-encoded-backslash payloads returned HTTP 200 with the secret leaked; after the fix both return 404, while the forward-slash control request and a legitimate file request behave unchanged.
